title: Shakuntala
hook: a king calls out at an empty hermitage, and the woman who answers sets terms before she says yes

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakuntala as a newborn by the river, guarded by birds and named for them by Kanva.

Who is here? That's the first thing King Dushyanta says at the hermitage. He has been hunting, has left his soldiers behind, and walks into the quiet place where the sage Kanva lives and calls out. Kanva isn't home. A young woman comes out instead, dressed like an ascetic, and welcomes him the way a host should. Then the king proposes marriage, almost at once, and the story waits to see what she'll say. What she says is not quite yes.
screen: `WHO IS HERE?` → `THE SAGE IS AWAY.` → `NOT QUITE YES.`

segments.voice: First, the welcome. Shakuntala offers the king a seat and water and asks after his health, the duties of a host, and tells him her father has gone to gather fruit. Wait, she says; he'll be back soon. The king asks who she is, and she tells him her birth: the sage, the apsara, the birds. Then he asks her to marry him. Her first answer is patience. Wait for my father, she says. He will give me to you. The king answers with law. There is a form of marriage called the gandharva, he says, made by two people's own choice, and it's lawful for a king. She can give herself. And here Shakuntala does the thing the rest of her story hangs on. She agrees, on one condition: promise that the son born of me will be your heir and rule after you. Only if you promise this. The king promises. They marry. He leaves for his city, saying he'll send a proper escort to bring her to the palace. Then Kanva comes home. The epic says he knows what happened through his own inner sight, and he isn't angry. He's glad, blesses her, and tells her the marriage is a good one. Time goes by. She gives birth to a son, who grows up in the hermitage so strong he tames the wild animals of the forest; the hermits call him the all-tamer. And from the city, nobody comes. Hold on to the condition she set. Young, alone, asked by a king, she didn't just say yes. She asked for a promise, out loud. Tomorrow, she carries that promise into court.
screen: `SHE WELCOMES HIM AS A HOST` · `WAIT FOR MY FATHER` · `YES, IF YOU PROMISE ME THIS` · `THE BOY GROWS, AND NO ONE COMES`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you've agreed to lately: a plan, a job, a favor. Ask gently whether there was something you needed and didn't say, and let one simple sentence form, the way Shakuntala said hers; you don't have to send it anywhere, just hear it in your own voice. If you pray, you can bring it into prayer.
Shakuntala. The young woman who welcomed a king, asked him to wait, and then said yes only on a promise spoken aloud.
Your line: Shakuntala. Her yes came with a promise attached, spoken out loud. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus know this part of Shakuntala's story from the Mahabharata's first book, the Adi Parva, where the meeting and the gandharva marriage take place at Kanva's hermitage.

original.note: Sanskrit: the gandharva form of marriage, made by the couple's own choice, which Dushyanta proposes to Shakuntala.

chat.says: Did Shakuntala just say yes when the king asked to marry her?
options: Not quite: she asked him to wait for Kanva, then agreed if her son would be heir.
Yes, she said yes at once, since he was the king and she couldn't refuse.
No, Kanva came home first and arranged the whole wedding himself.
chat.meaning: She first asked the king to wait for her father, then agreed to the gandharva marriage only on his promise about her son.

Dushyanta.meaning: the king who comes to Kanva's hermitage

gandharva.meaning: a marriage made by two people's own choice

apsara.meaning: a celestial dancer, like Shakuntala's mother

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Dushyanta at Kanva's hermitage; Shakuntala's welcome; his proposal; the gandharva marriage; her condition that her son be heir; Kanva's return and blessing; the birth and boyhood of her son)

notes: Confirm the order: welcome, her birth told, proposal, 'wait for my father', the king's account of the gandharva form, her condition (her son to be heir apparent), his promise, his promise to send an escort. The epic numbers the forms of marriage; the count was left out.
Confirm Kanva knows by inner (spiritual) sight and approves. The boon she asks of him was left out.
'The all-tamer': the boy's name Sarvadamana as the hermits give it; the Sanskrit name was left out of the voice so as not to step on day 1352, which names him Bharata.
The epic says the boy grows for some years in the hermitage before Kanva sends them to court; the span was left out under the claims rule.
